entries.clue: At home, looked after child, one practised in being greedy (10)

blocks.note: somebody at home is in, as in 'she's in this evening'
to sit for someone is to mind their child for the evening
i is the Roman numeral for one
practised at a job means able at it, skilled through repetition

annotation.surface: A stay-at-home babysitter who has grown rather good at the work.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Looked after child' hides an everyday verb: to sit for someone is to babysit, and parents still say they sat for the neighbours. 'Practised' is the adjective meaning skilled, not a past tense.
annotation.definitionFit: Insatiable describes an appetite that nothing will satisfy, so it is greed carried to the point where it cannot be fed.

entries.clue: Idlers play vacuous game (1-3)

indicatorNotes.vacuous: Vacuous means empty inside, so each word it touches keeps only the letters at its two ends.

blocks.note: the word emptied of everything between its first and last letters
the same treatment, leaving the letters it opens and closes with

annotation.surface: Layabouts filling an afternoon with a mindless game.
annotation.walkthrough: One instruction is being applied to two words in a row, which is what makes four letters this awkward. I-spy is the children's guessing game — 'I spy with my little eye, something beginning with...'.
annotation.definitionFit: I-spy is a named game, the one families play in the car, so the flat noun 'game' covers it.

entries.clue: Hauls up teacher's pet (4)

indicatorNotes.up: In a down entry the letters run downwards, so anything sent up is read back the other way.

blocks.note: hauls means tows, and the tow truck's word climbs back up the grid

annotation.surface: A breakdown truck dragging away something the teacher is fond of.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hauls' looks like a verb the sentence needs and is the whole of the wordplay. In British schools a swot is the pupil who works relentlessly, and gets no thanks from the class for it.
annotation.definitionFit: The swot is the pupil always ahead with the homework, so the staff room's favourite and the playground's standing insult are the same child.

entries.clue: Royal High let out sought-after silverware (3,4,5)

indicatorNotes.out: Out of order is what the word means here, so the letters in front of it go back in a different arrangement.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, twelve letters

annotation.surface: A school called Royal High finishing for the day.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital letters make Royal High look like a name to be respected rather than letters to be broken up, and 'let out' finishes the illusion. Knights of the Round Table spent whole careers on this hunt.
annotation.definitionFit: The Holy Grail is the cup of the Last Supper, chased across Europe by legend for centuries, which makes it tableware nobody has ever stopped wanting.

entries.clue: Naked, vast rider atop horse like so (7)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is adverbial rather than a noun or verb: it points at the posture the word names instead of offering a synonym for it.

indicatorNotes.Naked: Stripped of its covering, a phrase loses the letters at its outside edges and shows what was underneath.

blocks.note: seven letters running on across the gap, with the opening v and closing r stripped off

annotation.surface: An unclothed rider perched on an enormous horse.
annotation.walkthrough: The run of letters crosses the space between two words, which is where hidden answers are hardest to see. 'Naked' belongs to the rider in the picture and to the spelling in the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: To sit astride something is to sit with a leg down either side of it, which is exactly how a rider sits on a horse.

entries.clue: Sign with frustrated announcement posted up that suits acrobat (7)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a verb phrase saying what the answer does for an acrobat, not a noun that could be swapped in for it.

indicatorNotes.posted up: Something posted up travels towards the top, and in a down entry that means those letters are read backwards.

blocks.note: Leo is one of the twelve signs of the zodiac
'drat' is the small exclamation of frustration, sent back up the grid

annotation.surface: A zodiac sign beside an exasperated notice pinned to a wall.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drat' is the mild British curse the clue wants, and it is only useful once it is read the other way round. 'Sign' is the astrological sense, not a signature or a noticeboard.
annotation.definitionFit: A leotard is the one-piece stretch garment a gymnast or circus performer works in, so it is literally the thing that suits an acrobat.

entries.clue: Regularly outspends - what's new? - the reverse (4)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition works by contradiction rather than synonym: it names the opposite of the answer and then tells you to take the opposite of that.

indicatorNotes.Regularly: Taken at regular intervals means every second letter is picked up and the ones between are left.

blocks.note: every second letter of oUtSpEnDs, starting from the second

annotation.surface: A weary shrug at somebody who always manages to outspend everyone.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The reverse' looks like a turnaround instruction and is nothing of the kind: it flips the meaning of 'new', not the order of any letters. Nothing in the clue is read backwards.
annotation.definitionFit: Something used is second-hand and has had an owner already, which is the plain opposite of new.

entries.clue: Unfashionable origin of itself, for one? (6,4)

annotation.definition: Unfashionable origin of itself, for one?

blocks.note: square is the old slang for somebody hopelessly behind the fashion
the root of a matter is where it started, its origin

annotation.walkthrough: The question mark is the signal that an example is coming, and the example is the number one — the only positive number whose square root is itself. 'Square' meaning out of date is the joke underneath the arithmetic.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight the whole sentence is true of one: its square root is one again, so the thing named really is the origin of itself for that number.

entries.clue: DIYer uses these ... these studs for reparation (4,6)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a whole clause with the answer as its object, rather than a noun phrase that could stand in its place.

indicatorNotes.for reparation: Something sent for repair is taken apart and put back together differently, which is what happens to these letters.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

annotation.surface: A home improver reaching for the studs needed to mend something.
annotation.walkthrough: The ellipsis is the setter owning up to the repetition: the first 'these' belongs to the definition and the second is fodder. Studs are the upright timbers inside a partition wall.
annotation.definitionFit: Dust sheets are the old cloths a decorator spreads over floors and furniture before opening a tin, so they are standard do-it-yourself kit.

entries.clue: Seeing yourself in others, as happens in cinema (10)

annotation.definitionNote: The second half describes rather than substitutes: it names what a cinema does instead of offering a noun that could replace the answer.

blocks.note: the psychological habit of pinning your own feelings onto other people
the beam thrown from the box at the back of the auditorium onto the screen

annotation.surface: The way filmgoers recognise themselves in the characters on screen.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma welds the two halves into one thought, which is the whole deception. Psychology borrowed the word from optics, where an image is thrown outward onto something else, so both senses share an ancestor.
annotation.definitionFit: Projection is the defence mechanism of attributing your own feelings to somebody else, and it is also the throwing of a film onto a screen.

entries.clue: Taps' defects (4)

blocks.note: to tap a line is to listen in on it secretly
the faults that stop a piece of software working

annotation.surface: Something wrong with the plumbing.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe is the trap: it binds the two words into one possessive phrase about leaky taps, and neither word is doing that job. Both senses of the answer trace back to the insect.
annotation.definitionFit: A bug is the hidden microphone used to tap a line, and equally the flaw lurking in a program, so both plurals answer to the same word.

entries.clue: Delivery notification from armourer in Meg Ryan film (5,3,4)

annotation.definitionNote: The first definition is a spoken sentence rather than a synonym: it is the announcement itself, which no single noun could replace.

blocks.note: mail is the linked metal a medieval armourer works in, so his consignment announces itself
the 1998 romantic comedy with Tom Hanks, titled after the email alert

annotation.surface: An armourer's delivery slip turning up in a romantic comedy.
annotation.walkthrough: The email alert that gave the film its name is the reading everyone reaches for first; the armourer restores the older sense of mail, the linked rings a knight wore into battle.
annotation.definitionFit: You've Got Mail is the Meg Ryan and Tom Hanks romance of 1998, and the same three words are what an armourer delivering chain mail would be telling you.

entries.clue: Where rappers may make for happy mediums? (5,6)

annotation.definition: Where rappers may make for happy mediums?

blocks.note: read as hip-hop artists heading somewhere, and meant as the spirits who answer a sitting by knocking
read as the idiom for a sensible compromise, and meant as the contented people running the sitting

annotation.surface: Hip-hop artists heading somewhere that keeps everybody reasonably content.
annotation.walkthrough: Victorian seances called a knocking spirit a rapper, which is the sense the clue needs and the modern one buries. 'Happy medium' is an idiom here split back into two separate words.
annotation.definitionFit: A ouija board is the lettered board a seance uses to take messages from the dead, so rapping spirits arrive there and a medium is glad of them.

entries.clue: Gaga, soused, pickled: your 'best friend', perhaps! (7,3)

indicatorNotes.pickled: Pickled is the drinker's word for thoroughly drunk, and nothing drunk stays in the order it was set down in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

annotation.surface: A friend being described as utterly sozzled, three times over.
annotation.walkthrough: Gaga, soused and pickled all mean drunk, so two of them are letters and only one can be the instruction. The sausage dog is the dachshund, named for its shape rather than its diet.
annotation.definitionFit: A dog is proverbially man's best friend, and the sausage dog is one breed of dog, which is what the 'perhaps' is flagging.

entries.clue: Cry about blokeish humour while cycling to university city (10)

indicatorNotes.about: What goes about a thing goes round the outside of it, so whatever is named next sits inside.
indicatorNotes.cycling: A wheel brings the same points round again in the same order, so the word's front letter is carried to the back.

blocks.note: the outer word, opened up after its first letter to take the rest
banter is the laddish back-and-forth, with its opening B carried round to the end
u is the standard abbreviation for university

annotation.surface: Someone grumbling about lads' joking as they ride to a university town.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cycling' is the bicycle in the picture and a letter-shift in the wordplay, and it acts on one word only. Canterbury is the Kent cathedral city, seat of the Archbishop and home to two universities.
annotation.definitionFit: Canterbury is a cathedral city in Kent, so the bare word 'city' defines it once 'university' has been taken away for its letter.

entries.clue: 'Don't trust Ms Karenina' said study (7)

indicatorNotes.said: What is said is heard rather than read, so the words before it are wanted for their sound and not their spelling.

blocks.note: Tolstoy's heroine is Anna Karenina, and the reason given for distrusting her is that Anna lies

annotation.surface: One friend warning another off Tolstoy's heroine.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue never writes her first name, so the warning only works once you supply it yourself. Ms Karenina is the tell: the title is modern and the novel is not.
annotation.definitionFit: To analyse something is to study it closely, taking it apart to see what it is made of.

entries.clue: Sundry seabirds skinned eel (7)

indicatorNotes.skinned: Skinning strips off the outside, so the word that follows loses the letter at each of its ends.

blocks.note: divers are the fish-hunting seabirds Americans call loons
with its outer e and l taken off, only the middle letter is left

annotation.surface: Assorted seabirds making short work of an eel.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Skinned' belongs to the eel in the picture and to the spelling in the wordplay. Divers are proper birds — great northern, red-throated — and not people in wetsuits.
annotation.definitionFit: Diverse means made up of several different kinds, which is what sundry says of a collection of things.

entries.clue: Touring, endlessly airsick: T Swift described as such (7)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition names the writer the adjective is habitually applied to rather than giving a synonym, so it describes the answer instead of replacing it.

indicatorNotes.Touring: A tour goes round and comes back another way, so the letters do not keep the order they were given.
indicatorNotes.endlessly: Something endless has no end, so the final letter of the word that follows is dropped before anything else happens.

blocks.note: the word with its closing k removed, as the instruction in front of it asks
the initial printed before the surname, taken simply as the letter it is

annotation.surface: Taylor Swift on tour, ill for the whole flight.
annotation.walkthrough: The initial belongs to Taylor on the surface and to Jonathan in the answer: Swift wrote Gulliver's Travels and A Modest Proposal, the models of English satire. 'Touring' is the shuffle, not a journey.
annotation.definitionFit: Jonathan Swift's writing is the standard example of savage mockery in English, so this is the adjective critics reach for whenever they describe him.

entries.clue: Creature; equine netherwards, then Adamite upper region, primarily? (7)

annotation.definition: Creature; equine netherwards, then Adamite upper region, primarily?

indicatorNotes.primarily: What comes primarily comes first, so every word in front gives up only the letter it opens with.

blocks.clueFragment: Creature; equine netherwards, then Adamite upper region
blocks.note: seven words handing over their opening letters in the order they are written

annotation.surface: A being described from the ground up: horse below, man above.
annotation.walkthrough: Adamite means a descendant of Adam, which is to say a human being, and netherwards means towards the lower parts. The sentence describes the thing and spells it at the same time.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight it is an accurate description of the Greek myth: a centaur is horse from the shoulders back and man from the shoulders up.

entries.clue: Spouting madly, forgets name and and scoffs freely (4,3)

indicatorNotes.madly: Done madly, a thing is done without order, so the letters will not stay as they were set down.
indicatorNotes.forgets: What is forgotten is no longer there, so the letter named next drops out before the rest are rearranged.

blocks.note: the eight letters of the word once the n has gone
n is the abbreviation for name, and it is the letter the instruction takes out

annotation.surface: Somebody ranting away, losing a name mid-sentence and then tucking in.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Scoffs' is the British word for eating fast, not for mocking, which is the reading the ranting surface pushes. Spouting is what the clue pretends to be about and where every letter comes from.
annotation.definitionFit: To pig out is to eat greedily and without restraint, which is what scoffing freely amounts to.

entries.clue: Some HP ink - gingerly, might you drink it? (4,3)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a question with 'it' standing for the letters just found, rather than a noun phrase that could replace the answer.

indicatorNotes.Some: Some of a thing is a part of it taken as it stands, so an unbroken run of the letters in front is what is wanted.

blocks.note: seven letters running on from the middle of HP straight through into gingerly

annotation.surface: Somebody eyeing a drop of HP's ink and wondering, cautiously, whether it is drinkable.
annotation.walkthrough: HP is a printer maker to one reader and a bottle of brown sauce to another, and neither matters: the letters simply run on across the dash. Pink gin is gin with a few drops of Angostura bitters.
annotation.definitionFit: Pink gin is a real drink, the Royal Navy's gin tinted with Angostura bitters, so the question the clue asks answers itself yes.

entries.clue: Tornado king condemned as 'unsolvable problem' (7,4)

indicatorNotes.condemned: A condemned building is pulled down, and letters condemned come apart the same way and go back up in another arrangement.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters

annotation.surface: A king nicknamed Tornado written off as a hopeless case.
annotation.walkthrough: The quotation marks are the setter admitting the definition is a figure of speech rather than a dictionary entry. Alexander the Great met the knot at Gordium and cut it instead of untying it.
annotation.definitionFit: A Gordian knot is the byword for a tangle too intricate to be picked apart, which is why the only answer anyone found to it was a sword.

entries.clue: Everyman given tips in amateur theatre, being a ham? (4)

annotation.definitionNote: Ham is one kind of meat rather than a word for meat in general, and the question mark is the setter's flag for defining by example.

indicatorNotes.tips: The tip of a thing is its very point, so each word that follows yields only the letter it starts with.

blocks.note: Everyman is the name this setter signs, so he is talking about himself
taking only the opening letter of each of these two words, which is the operation the instruction asked for

annotation.surface: The setter picking up pointers down at the local am-dram society.
annotation.walkthrough: Everyman is the pseudonym printed above this puzzle, so the setter is naming himself inside his own clue. A ham is an actor who overplays, which is what keeps the amateur theatre in the sentence.
annotation.definitionFit: Ham is cured pig, one of the meats on the counter, so the clue reaches the general word through a particular one.

entries.clue: Burn most of leafy green vegetable (4)

indicatorNotes.most of: Most of a word is not all of a word, so the letter at the end is left behind.

blocks.note: the vegetable wanted is the five-letter one with thick white stalks, and the instruction in front removes its closing letter

annotation.surface: A cook told to scorch most of a bunch of greens.
annotation.walkthrough: Swiss chard is the leaf vegetable with thick white stalks, a fixture of British allotments. 'Most of' is the whole of the instruction and it costs the word only its last letter.
annotation.definitionFit: To char something is to scorch it black, which is burning it without burning it away.

entries.clue: Instrument found at end of canal? (4)

annotation.definitionNote: The second half describes where the thing sits instead of naming it, which is what the question mark is apologising for.

blocks.note: the skin stretched over a shell and beaten with sticks
the taut membrane sealing the inner end of the ear canal

annotation.surface: A musical instrument dredged up at the end of a waterway.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Canal' wants to be the waterway with a narrowboat on it, and the canal meant here is inside your head. Anatomy really does call that membrane the drum, not only the eardrum.
annotation.definitionFit: A drum is the struck instrument of any percussion section, and the drum is equally the membrane closing off the far end of the ear canal.

entries.clue: Commercial plugging bracelet and pipe down in S Asian state (10)

indicatorNotes.plugging: A plug is pushed into a hole, so whatever is plugging something ends up inside it.

blocks.note: a bangle is the rigid bracelet worn on the wrist
a commercial is an ad
sh is the noise you make telling somebody to be quiet

annotation.surface: An advert pushing a bracelet, and an order to keep the noise down.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Plugging' is the advertiser's word for pushing a product and the wordplay's word for pushing letters inside another word. 'Pipe down' is the navy's order to stop the racket, sounded on the bosun's pipe.
annotation.definitionFit: Bangladesh is the country on the Bay of Bengal east of India, so naming its corner of the map identifies it.

entries.clue: Pretence detectable by auditor, chaps (4)

indicatorNotes.detectable by auditor: An auditor is one who listens, so the word in front is to be caught by ear and then written down as it sounded.

blocks.note: a guise is the false appearance somebody puts on, and the two words are said identically

annotation.surface: A sham that the accountants would spot at once, lads.
annotation.walkthrough: An auditor audits accounts, but the word itself comes from hearing, and that older sense is the one in play. 'Guise' now survives almost only in the phrase 'in the guise of'.
annotation.definitionFit: Guys is the everyday plural for men, which is what chaps means on this side of the Atlantic.

entries.clue: One whose work might be a ... travail? (10)

annotation.definition: One whose work might be a ... travail?

blocks.note: read as the job a person does, and meant as a single English word handed over to be turned into another language
travail is the French for work, so this is what comes back, the ellipsis covering the pause while it is done

annotation.surface: Somebody whose job might well turn out to be a struggle.
annotation.walkthrough: Travail in English means toil, which is the reading the surface wants. In French it is nothing more dramatic than the word for work, and the clue is showing the answer doing its job on 'work' itself.
annotation.definitionFit: A translator turns a word into its equivalent in another tongue, and 'work' put into French comes back as travail — the clue is a sample of that job.
